prize_parts.citation: For transforming the measurement of intergenerational mobility with population-scale administrative data, and for design-based evidence on how childhood environment and place shape economic opportunity.

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed from B022 (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) to B002 (Chetty, Hendren, Friedman). My assessment of the science in B022 is unchanged: it solved a concrete estimation problem and has three decades of use. Two things moved me. First, I tried to apply one weighting to all candidates: originality, quality of identification, durability, and how tractable the attribution is. Under it, B002 is the only candidate that scores well on all four. It created a new empirical object, place-specific mobility measured on population records. Its designs (movers, childhood exposure) can be inspected by others. Its measurement standard has already been taken up with other administrative datasets. The mobility and place-effects papers have a recurring lead trio. Second, in round 1 I argued against B002 mainly on maturity and diffuse team credit. Having read the exchange, I think the maturity objection applies mostly to long-run causal claims about specific place effects and much less to the measurement and design contribution. A citation limited to measurement and exposure-based designs does not rest on the contested claims. I also had a consistency problem. I praised BLP as a methodological advance that made a practice feasible on real data, and it would be inconsistent to discount B002 as 'mere measurement'. The two are the same kind of contribution: tools that let a field observe and estimate something it could not before. B022 has an attribution issue of its own (Bresnahan's precursor work, and the loose fit of the dynamic-industry strand). I do not treat the opening support count as scientific merit. I will say plainly that my choice of what to vote for in a private ballot does take into account which configurations can realistically be decided, and that this is a practical consideration, not a scientific one. I keep B022 as an alternative because I still think it deserves a prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations on B002 remain. The core results are roughly 2014 to 2022, and the causal interpretation of neighbourhood and exposure effects, and the noise in small-area estimates, are still being tested. Identification rests on assumptions (for example, that movers' outcomes reflect exposure and not selection) that are credible but not settled. The programme is a large team effort, so any three-name cut is a judgement, and Katz, who has Moving to Opportunity and is credited on the ballot, is left out. A committee could reasonably wait. On the other candidates, B027 has the longest test and a concentrated credit structure but weaker cross-country identification. B015 has a diffuse attribution problem and a Calvo core that fits micro price data only partly. B004 has overlap with the 2022 prize. I also work in industrial organisation, and that familiarity may make me favour method contributions that estimate something from data, which could bias me toward B002 and B022 over theory-led candidates.

responses.point: Boppart keeps Katz off the three-name cap because Moving to Opportunity is an input to the causal neighbourhood question and the mobility reanalysis was done by the Chetty-Hendren-Friedman group. He asks which of the three names an argument for Katz would displace.
responses.response: I agree with that way of framing the Katz question, and it answers the chair's question for me. I have not seen an argument on the evidence that displaces Chetty, Hendren or Friedman, and swapping in Katz would shift the discovery being rewarded toward the experimental strand. I would not table a separate Katz-inclusive configuration unless a colleague argues it on those terms. I also take your point that 'a decade old' is not 'untested'. I weigh it somewhat differently from how I did in my own round 1. The part of the record I find durable is the measurement and the designs. The part I would keep out of the citation is any claim about long-run policy effects of moving.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B002 seventh. He worries the findings may prove data-driven rather than foundational, and that Chetty's wider oeuvre, including the tax work (B037), may be judged as one body of work. He still treats B002 as a major empirical advance and lists it as an alternative.
responses.response: I held a version of this worry in round 1, so I am not dismissing it. What moved me is that I do not think 'foundational' should mean only a theory result. BLP is also a method for estimating something, and I would credit it as a prize-level contribution on the same grounds. If the committee accepts that kind of contribution in one field, it should accept it here. On B037, I agree with Boppart and Dreber-Almenberg that the citation should be written around the mobility discovery, and that any overlap with Chetty's other work be stated openly. Where I still agree with you is on the weight of time: B015 has decades of confirmation that B002 cannot match. That is a real difference, but I do not think it decides the comparison once B015's attribution is taken into account.

responses.point: Hassler replied to my round 1 position on B015 by saying the Calvo device is a tractable framework refined against micro evidence, including our own menu-cost work, and that the citation should be broad: nominal rigidities and policy rules, not time-dependent pricing alone. He also argues earlier macro prizes covered expectations and credibility, not price-setting and rule design.
responses.response: I accept the point about earlier prizes. I over-weighted overlap, and I now think the nominal-rigidity core is not covered by Lucas, Kydland-Prescott or Sargent-Sims. A broad citation also reduces my empirical concern. I would still not put B015 first, for two reasons. The cut among Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler cannot be made on a criterion I can verify. Second, the menu-cost paper you mention shows that asymmetric and state-dependent adjustment matter in the data, and I do not think a prize should rest on a pricing device the micro evidence only partly supports. I disclose that I co-authored that paper with you, so my view here is not independent of yours, and I read your reply with that in mind.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson's citation says the work identifies how childhood environment and place causally shape opportunity. She argues the unresolved questions concern the size and interpretation of specific place effects and not the measurement advance or design approach, and she warns against overclaiming on long-run policy conclusions.
responses.response: I agree with that split and it shapes my citation. I deliberately wrote 'design-based evidence on how childhood environment and place shape economic opportunity' and left out 'causally', since that is the word the committee will be asked to defend under scrutiny. The chair's summary notes that the supporters word the citation differently. My preference is the narrower wording. It still credits the exposure and mover designs and the measurement standard. It does not claim that the causal question is closed. I would accept the stronger wording if colleagues who know the evidence better than I do judge it established.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B002 sixth because the core work is recent, long-run follow-up is still accumulating, and credit within a large team is hard to divide. He lists it as a strong alternative and resists letting first-place counts stand in for the open causal question.
responses.response: I share that last point. Support counts do not answer the long-run causal question, and I have tried not to let them. Where I differ from my own round 1 position is on how much the open question matters for the discovery named in the citation. If the award is for measurement and for designs that others can check, long-run follow-up refines the estimates but does not undo the contribution. If the committee wants the causal claims settled before recognising the work, then your timing objection is right, and B027 or B004 would be a natural alternative on the evidence. I would want that stated as a judgement about maturity and not as a doubt about quality.

uncertainties: Whether replication of exposure-effect estimates in non-US administrative data and further long-run follow-up are enough to treat the design-based findings as settled. I have not checked any of this independently.
Whether the contribution will be judged primarily measurement rather than a conceptual advance, and whether the committee applies that standard even-handedly across fields (B002 and B022 alike).
Whether Katz should replace one of the three names. I have not seen an evidence-based argument for it, but the Moving to Opportunity link is a real input.
Whether my change from B022 to B002 reflects my reassessment or an over-adjustment for the practical situation. I tried to separate the two, but I cannot rule out some influence.
My B002 judgement depends on general knowledge of the literature and the supplied files, and I have not verified citations or replication results.
statement.conflict_note: No listed co-author or institutional tie to Chetty, Hendren, Friedman or Katz appears in my profile, and none to Berry, Levinsohn or Pakes (B022) or to Persson, Tabellini or Besley (B027). I co-authored with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen (IJIO 2026, menu costs), which is adjacent to the price-rigidity theme of B015, a candidate I do not propose. My field, industrial organisation, is close to B022, which I now list only as an alternative, and I disclose that my familiarity may colour my view of method contributions. My spouse's public political role is a public fact, and my profile shows no bearing on any shortlisted candidate. One colleague's note refers to Persson's past committee service as having been disclosed in my opening, but my round 1 conflict note does not mention it and my profile does not establish it. I make no claim about it. I do not adjudicate any of these disclosures.
